body: Wayne Rooney has officially been confirmed as a contestant on this year’s I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here.
After weeks of speculation, the Manchester United and England legend is now set to take part in the 26th series of the popular reality show – two years after his wife Coleen’s successful stint .
Wayne Rooney is the latest sporting star to head into the I’m A Celeb camp ITV / Joel Anderson
In 2024, Coleen reached the final Down Under, and rumours had been rife that Wayne would be following in her footsteps this year.
While the Premier League icon remained tight-lipped on this talk, his participation has now been made official.
With a week to go until the next edition of I’m A Celebrity gets underway, Rooney ‘s appearance in the upcoming show was confirmed on Tuesday evening on the show’s official X account.
The ITV show shared a picture of this year’s contestants, where the 41-year-old can be seen front and centre amongst a host of stars.

While Rooney is undoubtedly the standout name, he will be joined in the jungle by comedian Leigh Francis – best known as Keith Lemon – as well as actress Joanna Page, who plays Stacey in the popular sitcom Gavin and Stacey.
Also among the big names heading to Australia this year is Love Island star Chloe Burrows.
Rooney ‘I’m A Celeb’ pay revealed
Rooney is reportedly set to earn more than anybody else on I’m A Celebrity this year, but surprisingly this will be less than what his wife Coleen picked up in 2024.
According to showbiz account ‘Super TV’ on X, the football great’s paycheque will be a huge £700,000 less than his other half’s.
Rooney is reportedly set to earn £800,000 for his time on I’m A Celeb, with the second-highest paid contestant this year being Kaiser Chiefs singer Ricky Wilson, who will reportedly earn £175,000.
Meanwhile, Coleen remains the joint-highest paid contestant of all time – with reports claiming she pocketed £1.5million for her stint two years ago, the same as politician Nigel Farage in 2023.
View Tweet: https://t.co/KTlku4vVaQ
Coleen was the first in the Rooney household to take on the I’m A Celebrity jungle Rex
As for Rooney, his earnings will place him third on the all-time list of contestants, while this is more than a number of other sporting stars.
Former Olympian Caitlyn Jenner and legendary ex-Premier League boss Harry Redknapp are each believed to have been paid £500,000.
Just behind them are Arsenal great Ian Wright and former boxing champion Amir Khan – who were both paid £400,000 for their participation in the show.
Rooney: Time is finally right
After his stint in the jungle was confirmed, Rooney revealed he’d only be listening to some of wife Coleen’s advice when on the show.
Man United’s all-time top goalscorer said: “Yeah, she has told me a bit of advice and I’ve had friends that have been in it as well.
“But I suppose you have to experience it yourself, don’t you?
Rooney has been working as a pundit since his last managerial stint at Plymouth ended in December 2024 Getty
“I’m just looking forward to experiencing it in my own way – I think that’s the most important thing.”

Rooney also revealed he had long thought about taking part in the show and explained now is finally the right time to sign up – having not held a managerial role since his sacking by Plymouth in 2024.
He added: “It’s a show I’ve always wanted to do.
“Me and Coleen would sit there watching and we both always said: ‘If we were going to do one, it’s the show to do’.
“Coleen did it a couple of years ago and then this year it came
about because of the way it fell – me not being great as a manager!
“And obviously not working full time as a player has given me time where I could do it, so I thought, why not?”

articles.headline: Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now
keyFacts: Tanuki: Pon's Summer launched today as a mail delivery and bike simulation game set in the Japanese countryside.
Players deliver mail on a BMX bike to earn money used to customise and restore a local shrine before summer ends.
The game includes minigames like baseball, sumo wrestling, sushi preparation, and fishing to help players interact with local characters.
body: Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

articles.headline: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
keyFacts: The United States boycotted a United Nations human rights review for the second consecutive year, becoming the only member state to do so twice.
ACLU human rights director Jamil Dakwar stated that the administration continued to violate human rights regarding immigrants, protesters, and the LGBTQ community.
The United Nations postponed deliberations on how to handle the U.S. absence until early next year.
body: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.
As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."
